herbs.name: Ginger
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Gingerols and shogaols inhibit COX-2 and 5-LOX (dual eicosanoid suppression) and antagonise gut 5-HT3 receptors, which is the main proposed anti-nausea route; fresh rhizome also carries zingibain, a cysteine protease (bromelain-like meat tenderiser), though it is not the active anti-emetic principle.
herbs.evidence_note: Reasonable trial support for pregnancy nausea (included in the Cochrane review of NVP interventions, with low-certainty but consistent benefit) and an EMA well-established/traditional monograph for motion sickness; evidence for arthritis pain is weaker.
herbs.dose: Nausea: 1-1.5 g dried ginger powder per day in divided doses (studied range 0.5-2 g); motion sickness (EMA): 1-2 g powdered rhizome 30-60 min before travel. Tea: 1-2 g sliced fresh root steeped 10 min.
warnings: Additive bleeding risk is theoretical-to-modest with anticoagulants/antiplatelets (warfarin, clopidogrel) at >4 g/day; stop 1-2 weeks before surgery as a precaution
Heartburn, reflux and loose stool at high doses
Pregnancy: studied doses up to ~1 g/day look safe; avoid large supplemental doses near term
Gallstones: use caution (cholagogue)
herbs.element_or_dosha: TCM: fresh (sheng jiang) pungent and slightly warm; dried (gan jiang) pungent and hot. Ayurveda: 'vishwabhesaj' (universal medicine), katu rasa, ushna virya, pacifies Vata and Kapha, may aggravate Pitta.
herbs.folk_correspondence: No separate Culpeper entry; listed among his simples ('Zingiberis... helps digestion, warms the stomach'). Modern Western-herbal lists assign Mars.

herbs.name: Peppermint
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Menthol blocks L-type calcium channels in intestinal smooth muscle (antispasmodic) and activates TRPM8 cold receptors; peppermint oil mildly inhibits CYP3A4 in vitro, of uncertain clinical size.
herbs.evidence_note: A 2019 meta-analysis of 12 RCTs (835 patients) found enteric-coated peppermint oil beat placebo for global IBS symptoms (NNT about 3) and abdominal pain (NNT about 4); EMA has a well-established-use monograph for the oil.
herbs.dose: IBS: 0.2-0.4 mL (about 180-225 mg) enteric-coated peppermint oil, 2-3 times daily before meals for up to 3 months. Tea: 1.5-3 g leaf per cup, 3 times daily. Headache: 10% oil in ethanol on temples.
warnings: Reflux/heartburn (relaxes lower oesophageal sphincter); non-enteric-coated oil worsens it
Do not apply oil to the face or chest of infants and young children: menthol can trigger laryngospasm/apnoea
Enteric coating dissolves early with antacids, PPIs or H2 blockers - separate by 2 h
Essential oil is toxic if swallowed neat in quantity
Gallstones/bile-duct obstruction: avoid oil
herbs.element_or_dosha: TCM (bo he, Mentha haplocalyx): pungent, cool; disperses wind-heat. Ayurveda: cooling, pacifies Pitta and Kapha.
herbs.folk_correspondence: Venus (Culpeper, 'Mint: It is an herb of Venus')

herbs.name: German Chamomile
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Apigenin binds the benzodiazepine site of GABA-A receptors weakly and inhibits COX-2 expression; bisabolol and chamazulene are anti-inflammatory; chamomile inhibits CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 in vitro.
herbs.evidence_note: Small trials suggest modest benefit for generalized anxiety disorder (oral extract) but sleep evidence is thin; EMA recognises it as a traditional herbal medicine for minor GI complaints and mouth/skin inflammation.
herbs.dose: Tea: 2-4 g dried flower heads in 150 mL boiling water, covered 5-10 min, 3-4 times daily. Anxiety trials: 500 mg standardized extract 1-3 times daily (up to 1500 mg/day).
warnings: Allergy in people sensitive to Asteraceae (ragweed, daisy, marigold) - rare anaphylaxis
Possible additive bleeding with warfarin (case reports)
Additive sedation with benzodiazepines, alcohol, other sedatives
Ciclosporin and other CYP3A4 substrates: monitor
herbs.element_or_dosha: Ayurveda: cooling, calms Pitta and Vata. Unani: babuna, hot and dry in first degree.
herbs.folk_correspondence: Moon (Culpeper, 'Camomile... under the dominion of the Moon'); many later herbals instead give the Sun

herbs.name: Garlic
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Crushing triggers the enzyme alliinase to convert alliin to allicin within seconds (so chop and wait ~10 min before heating, which destroys alliinase); ajoene inhibits platelet aggregation, and garlic supplements lower saquinavir levels via CYP3A4/P-gp induction.
herbs.evidence_note: Meta-analyses show small BP reductions in hypertensive people and small lipid effects; the Cochrane review on preventing colds rests on a single trial and is insufficient.
herbs.dose: 1 fresh clove (about 2-5 g) daily; or 600-1200 mg dried garlic powder daily in divided doses; or aged garlic extract 600-2400 mg daily.
warnings: Bleeding risk with warfarin/antiplatelets and before surgery (stop 7-10 days prior)
Reduces blood levels of saquinavir and possibly other HIV protease inhibitors
Raw garlic on skin can cause chemical burns
Heartburn, body/breath odour
herbs.element_or_dosha: TCM (da suan): pungent, warm. Ayurveda (lasuna): five tastes except sour, hot; reduces Vata and Kapha, aggravates Pitta.
herbs.folk_correspondence: Mars (Culpeper, 'Mars owns this herb... the poor man's treacle')

herbs.name: Turmeric
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Curcumin suppresses NF-kB signalling and COX-2/LOX expression, and inhibits CYP3A4, CYP2C9 and UGT glucuronidation; its own bioavailability is very low because it is rapidly glucuronidated - piperine (black pepper) blocks that glucuronidation and raises plasma curcumin roughly 20-fold.
herbs.evidence_note: Several small trials support knee-osteoarthritis pain relief comparable to NSAIDs, but most claims (cancer, depression, Alzheimer's) are unproven, and LiverTox now documents over a dozen cases of turmeric-supplement liver injury, especially with piperine-enhanced products.
herbs.dose: Culinary: 1-3 g turmeric powder/day is typical dietary intake. Osteoarthritis trials: 500-2000 mg curcumin extract/day in divided doses for 8-12 weeks. EMA traditional use: 1.5-3 g dried rhizome per day.
warnings: Liver injury reported with concentrated supplements (LiverTox), higher risk with piperine/bioavailability-enhanced forms
Antiplatelet effect - caution with anticoagulants
CYP3A4/2C9 inhibition: may raise levels of drugs like tacrolimus, some chemotherapies
Gallstones/bile-duct obstruction: avoid (cholagogue)
May lower blood sugar with diabetes drugs; iron absorption reduced
herbs.element_or_dosha: TCM (jiang huang): pungent, bitter, warm; moves blood and qi. Ayurveda (haridra): tikta and katu rasa, ushna virya; balances all three doshas, especially Kapha.

herbs.name: Honey (cough and wound)
herbs.latin: Mel (from Apis mellifera); medical-grade Manuka from Leptospermum scoparium nectar
uses: acute cough in children over 1 year
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Bee-added glucose oxidase slowly generates hydrogen peroxide when honey is diluted by wound fluid, while high sugar osmolarity and low pH inhibit bacteria; Manuka's non-peroxide activity comes from methylglyoxal (formed from nectar dihydroxyacetone). Heating destroys glucose oxidase.
herbs.evidence_note: Cochrane (2018, 6 RCTs, 899 children) found honey probably relieves cough symptoms better than no treatment, diphenhydramine or placebo and may be similar to dextromethorphan; for wounds, Cochrane finds honey heals partial-thickness burns faster than conventional dressings but evidence for other wounds is mixed.
herbs.dose: Cough: 2.5-10 mL (1/2-2 teaspoons) at bedtime for children over 1 year (age-scaled: 1-5 y 1/2 tsp, 6-11 y 1 tsp, 12+ 2 tsp). Wounds: sterile medical-grade honey dressing changed daily or as exudate requires - not kitchen honey on deep or infected wounds.
warnings: NEVER give honey to infants under 12 months - risk of infant botulism (Clostridium botulinum spores)
Raw kitchen honey is not sterile - use gamma-irradiated medical-grade honey on open wounds
Blood sugar: counts as sugar for diabetics
Bee/pollen allergy
'Mad honey' from Rhododendron nectar (grayanotoxins) causes bradycardia and hypotension
herbs.element_or_dosha: Ayurveda (madhu): sweet and astringent, heating when consumed, reduces Kapha; never to be cooked or heated per classical texts. Unani: hot and dry in second degree.

herbs.name: Elderberry
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Anthocyanins inhibit viral neuraminidase and haemagglutination in vitro; cooking matters because raw seeds, bark, leaves and unripe berries contain sambunigrin, which the plant enzyme beta-glucosidase hydrolyses to release hydrogen cyanide.
herbs.evidence_note: Mixed: a few small, often industry-funded trials suggested shorter flu duration, but a larger 2019 RCT found no benefit in influenza; NCCIH rates evidence as insufficient.
herbs.dose: Standardized syrup (e.g. Sambucol-type) studied at 15 mL four times daily for 5 days in adults; EMA traditional flower tea: 2-5 g dried flower per cup, up to 3 times daily.
warnings: Never eat raw berries, leaves, stems, bark or unripe fruit - cyanogenic glycosides cause vomiting, diarrhoea and in larger amounts cyanide poisoning; cook ripe berries thoroughly
Theoretical immunostimulant concern with immunosuppressants (transplant, autoimmune)
Insufficient pregnancy/breast-feeding data
Mild diuretic/laxative effect
herbs.folk_correspondence: Venus (Culpeper, 'Elder and Dwarf Tree are under the dominion of Venus')

herbs.name: Echinacea (purple coneflower)
herbs.latin: Echinacea purpurea (also E. angustifolia, E. pallida)
uses: short-term prevention and treatment of common cold
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Alkamides bind cannabinoid CB2 receptors on immune cells and modulate cytokine release; echinacea inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 but induces hepatic CYP3A4, a mixed net effect on drugs like midazolam.
herbs.evidence_note: Cochrane (24 RCTs) found products generally did not significantly beat placebo for treating colds, with a possible weak preventive effect; products vary wildly in species, part and extraction, which explains much of the inconsistency.
herbs.dose: E. purpurea pressed juice (aerial parts): 6-9 mL daily for up to 10 days at first symptoms (EMA). Dried root/extracts: commonly 300-500 mg 3 times daily, max 10 days for treatment.
warnings: Asteraceae allergy - rash and rare anaphylaxis; avoid in atopic people
Theoretical conflict with immunosuppressants; EMA advises against in progressive systemic/autoimmune disease (TB, MS, HIV, collagenoses)
Not for children under 12 (EMA) due to rash risk
Mixed CYP3A4 effects - monitor narrow-range drugs

herbs.name: White Willow Bark
herbs.latin: Salix alba (also S. purpurea, S. fragilis)
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Salicin is a prodrug: gut bacterial beta-glucosidases cleave it to saligenin, which the liver oxidises to salicylic acid, a weak reversible COX inhibitor - unlike aspirin it does not irreversibly acetylate platelet COX-1, so antiplatelet effect is milder and onset slower.
herbs.evidence_note: Cochrane's herbal-medicine-for-low-back-pain review found moderate evidence that willow bark extracts (120-240 mg salicin/day) reduce short-term pain better than placebo; osteoarthritis results are mixed. EMA lists it as well-established/traditional for back pain.
herbs.dose: Extract standardized to 120-240 mg salicin per day in divided doses (EMA up to 240 mg salicin/day), for up to 4 weeks. Decoction: 1-3 g dried bark simmered 10-15 min, up to 3-4 times daily (salicin content varies by species).
warnings: Salicylate allergy or aspirin-induced asthma: avoid
Children/teens with viral illness: theoretical Reye's syndrome risk - avoid
Additive effect with anticoagulants, antiplatelets, NSAIDs, methotrexate
Peptic ulcer, kidney disease, G6PD deficiency: caution
Pregnancy (third trimester) and breast-feeding: avoid
herbs.folk_correspondence: Moon (Culpeper, 'The Willow Tree... The Moon owns it')

herbs.name: Feverfew
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Parthenolide inhibits NF-kB and IKK, blocks platelet serotonin release, and modulates TRPA1 on trigeminal nerves; it also inhibits phospholipase A2-driven prostaglandin release.
herbs.evidence_note: Cochrane (6 trials, 561 people) found only a small preventive effect - about 0.6 fewer migraines a month - with low-quality evidence; EMA lists traditional use for migraine prophylaxis.
herbs.dose: Dried leaf powder 50-150 mg/day (often standardized to 0.2-0.4% parthenolide) taken continuously; benefit assessed after 4-6 weeks. Folk practice: 2-3 fresh leaves daily (chewing causes mouth ulcers in some).
warnings: Pregnancy: avoid (emmenagogue; historical abortifacient)
Asteraceae allergy
Antiplatelet effect - caution with anticoagulants
'Post-feverfew syndrome' on abrupt stop: rebound headache, anxiety, joint stiffness - taper
Mouth ulcers and tongue swelling from chewing fresh leaves
herbs.folk_correspondence: Venus (Culpeper, 'Venus commands this herb... to succour her sisters (women)')

herbs.name: Valerian
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Valerenic acid positively modulates GABA-A receptors containing beta2/beta3 subunits and inhibits GABA transaminase (the enzyme that breaks down GABA); in humans CYP effects are minor (no meaningful CYP3A4/2D6 change at normal doses).
herbs.evidence_note: Systematic reviews are inconsistent: some subjective sleep-quality improvement but objective sleep measures rarely change; EMA nonetheless grants well-established use for the ethanolic root extract.
herbs.dose: 300-600 mg root extract (or 2-3 g dried root as tea) 30 min-2 h before bed; effects build over 2-4 weeks.
warnings: Additive sedation with alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, opioids, other sedatives
Do not drive if drowsy
Rare liver injury reports (often multi-herb products)
Paradoxical stimulation/headache in some
Taper after long use; not for under-12s (EMA)
herbs.element_or_dosha: Ayurveda (tagara): bitter, pungent, heating; pacifies Vata and Kapha.
herbs.folk_correspondence: Mercury (Culpeper, 'Garden Valerian... under the influence of Mercury')

herbs.name: Lavender
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Linalool and linalyl acetate inhibit voltage-gated calcium channels and modulate GABA-A transmission; the standardized oral oil Silexan reduces serotonin-1A-related anxiety without benzodiazepine-like dependence.
herbs.evidence_note: Several RCTs of oral lavender oil (Silexan, 80-160 mg/day) show anxiety reduction similar to low-dose lorazepam or paroxetine in some trials; aromatherapy evidence is weaker and hard to blind.
herbs.dose: Anxiety: 80-160 mg standardized oral lavender oil (Silexan) once daily. Tea: 1-2 tsp dried flower per cup. Aromatherapy: 2-4 drops in diffuser. Topical: dilute 1-2% in carrier oil.
warnings: Additive sedation with CNS depressants
Oral capsules: burping, GI upset
Possible link between topical lavender/tea-tree products and prepubertal gynecomastia in boys (case series; disputed)
Contact dermatitis, especially oxidised oil
Essential oil should not be swallowed except as a formulated capsule
herbs.element_or_dosha: Unani (ustukhudus): hot and dry, a 'brain-cleanser'.
herbs.folk_correspondence: Mercury (Culpeper, 'Mercury owns the herb; and it carries his effects very potently')

herbs.name: St John's Wort
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Hyperforin is one of the most potent known natural agonists of the pregnane X receptor (PXR), strongly inducing CYP3A4, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and P-glycoprotein; it also broadly inhibits reuptake of serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine by raising intracellular sodium.
herbs.evidence_note: Cochrane (29 trials, 5489 patients) found standardized extracts better than placebo and similar to standard antidepressants for mild-to-moderate major depression, with fewer side effects; EMA grants well-established use.
herbs.dose: 300 mg extract (standardized to 0.3% hypericin and/or 3-5% hyperforin) three times daily (900 mg/day); allow 4-6 weeks.
warnings: MAJOR interactions via CYP3A4/P-gp induction: can cause failure of oral contraceptives (breakthrough pregnancy), transplant rejection (ciclosporin, tacrolimus), HIV treatment failure (protease inhibitors, NNRTIs), reduced warfarin, digoxin, irinotecan, imatinib, some statins and opioids
Serotonin syndrome with SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, tramadol, MAOIs - do not combine
Photosensitivity (hypericin), especially fair skin or with UV therapy
Can trigger mania in bipolar disorder
Induction persists ~2 weeks after stopping
herbs.folk_correspondence: Sun, in Leo (Culpeper, 'under the celestial sign Leo, and the dominion of the Sun')

herbs.name: Cranberry
uses: prevention of recurrent urinary tract infection
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: A-type proanthocyanidins block P-fimbriae adhesion of uropathogenic E. coli to bladder epithelium (anti-adhesion, not urine acidification); cranberry is a weak CYP2C9 inhibitor at most.
herbs.evidence_note: The 2023 Cochrane update (50 trials, 8857 people) concluded cranberry products reduce the risk of symptomatic UTI in women with recurrent UTIs, children, and after interventions - but not in elderly institutionalised people, pregnant women or people with neurogenic bladder. It does not treat an active infection.
herbs.dose: Prevention: products delivering about 36 mg PACs (DMAC/BL-DMAC method) daily, e.g. 240-300 mL 27% juice cocktail or standardized capsules (often 500 mg twice daily).
warnings: Not a treatment for active UTI or kidney infection - fever/flank pain needs antibiotics
Warfarin: case reports of raised INR; trials show small effect - monitor
Large amounts may raise oxalate kidney-stone risk
Juice cocktails are high in sugar
herbs.folk_correspondence: Culpeper has no cranberry entry; his related whortleberries are given to Jupiter

herbs.name: Fennel
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Anethole relaxes gut smooth muscle and has weak oestrogen-like activity; estragole is bioactivated by CYP1A2/2A6 to 1'-hydroxyestragole and then by sulfotransferase (SULT1A1) to a DNA-reactive ester - the reason EMA restricts long-term and child use.
herbs.evidence_note: Small trials suggest benefit for infant colic and dysmenorrhoea but are low-quality; EMA approves traditional use for mild spasmodic GI complaints.
herbs.dose: Adults: 1.5-2.5 g crushed seed infused as tea, 3 times daily (crush just before use). Do not exceed 2 weeks continuous use.
warnings: EMA: not recommended under 4 years and in pregnancy/breast-feeding because of estragole; avoid concentrated fennel oil
Celery/carrot/mugwort (Apiaceae) cross-allergy
Oestrogen-like activity: caution in hormone-sensitive cancers
Ciprofloxacin absorption reduced (animal data) - separate doses
herbs.element_or_dosha: Ayurveda (shatapushpa/saunf): sweet, cooling; balances all doshas, especially Pitta and Vata. Unani (badiyan): hot and dry in second degree. TCM (xiao hui xiang): pungent, warm.
herbs.folk_correspondence: Mercury, in Virgo (Culpeper, 'an herb of Mercury')

herbs.name: Clove
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Eugenol blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and activates/desensitises TRPV1 (local anaesthetic), inhibits COX-2, and inhibits platelet thromboxane synthesis; beta-caryophyllene is a CB2 agonist.
herbs.evidence_note: Eugenol is an established dental material (zinc oxide-eugenol dressings) and EMA lists clove oil for traditional temporary relief of dental pain; systemic claims are untested.
herbs.dose: Toothache: 1 drop clove oil on a cotton pellet applied to the cavity/affected area, up to 3 times daily for a few days (EMA). Culinary: whole/ground clove in food.
warnings: Undiluted oil can burn gums, mucosa and skin
Swallowing clove oil is dangerous in children: as little as 5-10 mL has caused liver failure, seizures and coma
Antiplatelet - caution with anticoagulants and before surgery
Not for dental abscess - see a dentist
herbs.element_or_dosha: TCM (ding xiang): pungent, warm; warms the middle and descends rebellious qi. Ayurveda (lavanga): katu and tikta rasa, cooling virya per some texts; reduces Kapha and Pitta. Unani (qaranful): hot and dry in third degree.
herbs.folk_correspondence: Culpeper's 'clove gilliflowers' are carnations, not the spice; no traditional Culpeper ruler for clove. Modern lists assign Jupiter.

herbs.name: Aloe vera
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: The inner gel contains a carboxypeptidase that degrades bradykinin (the 'bradykinase' anti-inflammatory activity) plus acemannan that stimulates fibroblasts; the yellow latex aloin is a prodrug cleaved by gut bacterial beta-glucosidases to aloe-emodin anthrone, a stimulant laxative.
herbs.evidence_note: Topical gel has some evidence for burns and psoriasis but results are mixed; oral latex laxatives were withdrawn from US OTC sale in 2002 over lack of safety data, and whole-leaf extract caused intestinal tumours in rats.
herbs.dose: Topical: apply fresh or commercial gel (inner leaf only) to the affected skin 2-3 times daily. Oral gel juice: products decolourised to <10 ppm aloin, commonly 30-60 mL/day; avoid latex.
warnings: Oral latex: cramping, diarrhoea, potassium loss - dangerous with digoxin, diuretics, corticosteroids
Oral aloe: case reports of acute hepatitis
May lower blood sugar - monitor on diabetes drugs
Pregnancy: oral latex can stimulate uterine contractions - avoid
Do not apply to deep or surgical wounds (one trial showed delayed healing)
herbs.element_or_dosha: Ayurveda (kumari/ghritkumari): bitter, sweet, cooling; pacifies Pitta and Kapha. TCM (lu hui, the dried latex): bitter, cold; purges heat.

herbs.name: Asian ginseng
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Ginsenosides are glycosides that gut bacteria de-glycosylate to active metabolites (e.g. Rb1 to compound K); ginseng increases nitric oxide synthase activity in vascular/erectile tissue and may induce CYP3A4 modestly in humans.
herbs.evidence_note: Some trials support erectile-function improvement and modest glucose lowering, but Cochrane found no convincing evidence of cognitive enhancement, and fatigue data are mixed.
herbs.dose: 200-400 mg standardized extract (4-7% ginsenosides) daily, or 1-2 g dried root daily; traditionally cycled (e.g. 2-3 weeks on, 1-2 weeks off). Red ginseng for ED trials: 900 mg 3 times daily.
warnings: Warfarin: reduced INR reported (ginseng lowered warfarin effect in a trial) - monitor
Insomnia, nervousness, headache; avoid with stimulants
May lower blood sugar - hypoglycaemia risk with insulin/sulfonylureas
Interaction reports with MAOI phenelzine (mania, headache)
Hypertension: caution at high doses ('ginseng abuse syndrome'); pregnancy: avoid (ginsenoside Rb1 teratogenic in animal embryos)
herbs.element_or_dosha: TCM (ren shen): sweet, slightly bitter, slightly warm (red ginseng warmer); greatly tonifies yuan qi, enters Spleen and Lung.

herbs.name: Ashwagandha
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Withanolides act as GABA-mimetics and lower cortisol by damping HPA-axis activity; withaferin A inhibits NF-kB and the proteasome; ashwagandha may raise thyroid hormone (T4) levels.
herbs.evidence_note: Multiple small RCTs (mostly from India, 8-12 weeks) show reduced perceived stress and cortisol, but certainty is low; LiverTox rates it a 'likely cause' (B) of clinically apparent liver injury, including rare fatal cases.
herbs.dose: Root extract 250-600 mg/day (e.g. KSM-66 300 mg twice daily) for 8-12 weeks; traditional churna 3-6 g root powder in warm milk at night.
warnings: Liver injury (cholestatic, 2-12 weeks after starting) - stop if jaundice, itching, dark urine; avoid with liver disease
Pregnancy: avoid (traditional abortifacient at high doses)
Thyroid: may raise T4 - caution with hyperthyroidism or levothyroxine
Additive sedation with benzodiazepines, alcohol
Immunosuppressants and autoimmune disease: theoretical immunostimulation; nightshade family allergy
herbs.element_or_dosha: Ayurveda: tikta, kashaya and madhura rasa, ushna virya; pacifies Vata and Kapha, may aggravate Pitta/ama in excess.

herbs.name: Holy Basil (Tulsi)
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Eugenol and ursolic acid inhibit COX-2; tulsi extracts lower cortisol in small trials and inhibit CYP enzymes (CYP2C9, CYP3A4) in vitro; it is the sacred plant of Vishnu/Lakshmi, grown in a tulsi vrindavan at Hindu homes.
herbs.evidence_note: MSKCC summarises small clinical studies suggesting reduced stress, anxiety and improved sleep and metabolic markers, but trials are short, small and heterogeneous.
herbs.dose: Tea: 1-2 tsp dried leaf (or 5-10 fresh leaves) per cup, 1-3 times daily. Trials: 300 mg-1 g leaf extract daily for 4-8 weeks.
warnings: May lower blood sugar - hypoglycaemia with diabetes drugs
Antiplatelet effect - caution with anticoagulants, before surgery
Pregnancy/conception: animal data show anti-fertility effects - avoid if trying to conceive
Contains methyl eugenol (a rodent carcinogen in isolated form) - favour moderate tea use over concentrated oils
herbs.element_or_dosha: Ayurveda: katu and tikta rasa, ushna virya; pacifies Kapha and Vata, increases Pitta.
herbs.folk_correspondence: Culpeper's 'Garden Basil' (O. basilicum, a different species) is given to Mars

herbs.name: Triphala (with Amla)
herbs.latin: Phyllanthus emblica (amla) + Terminalia chebula (haritaki) + Terminalia bellirica (bibhitaki)
uses: rasayana; amla as vitamin C-rich fruit
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Hydrolysable tannins (chebulinic, gallic acids) inhibit alpha-glucosidase and alpha-amylase and are antioxidants; anthraquinone-type glycosides in haritaki are hydrolysed by gut bacteria to mild laxative aglycones; triphala inhibits CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 in vitro.
herbs.evidence_note: Small trials support a mild laxative effect and plaque/gingivitis reduction as a mouthwash; amla trials show modest lipid and glucose improvements; large rigorous trials are lacking.
herbs.dose: Triphala churna 3-5 g (about 1 tsp) in warm water at bedtime, or 500-1000 mg tablets 1-2 times daily. Amla: 1-3 g dried fruit powder daily or one fresh fruit.
warnings: Diarrhoea and cramping at higher doses; avoid with active diarrhoea
Pregnancy: avoid (haritaki traditionally contraindicated)
May potentiate diabetes drugs and anticoagulants (amla antiplatelet effect)
Heavy-metal contamination has been found in some Ayurvedic products - buy tested brands
In-vitro CYP inhibition - caution with narrow-range drugs
herbs.element_or_dosha: Ayurveda: tridoshic - amla balances Pitta, haritaki Vata, bibhitaki Kapha; together five tastes except salty.

herbs.name: Licorice root
herbs.latin: Glycyrrhiza glabra (also G. uralensis in TCM)
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Glycyrrhizin is hydrolysed by gut bacteria to glycyrrhetinic acid, which inhibits 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 in the kidney so cortisol over-activates mineralocorticoid receptors - causing sodium retention, potassium loss and high blood pressure (pseudo-aldosteronism); deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) removes this.
herbs.evidence_note: EMA accepts traditional use for cough and dyspepsia; DGL ulcer evidence is old and limited; the mineralocorticoid toxicity is well established. LiverTox notes no clinically apparent liver injury.
herbs.dose: Cough/dyspepsia: 1.5-5 g dried root as decoction daily (EMA), keeping glycyrrhizin below about 100 mg/day and for no more than 4-6 weeks. DGL: 380-760 mg chewed 20 min before meals.
warnings: Hypertension, oedema, hypokalaemia (low potassium) and arrhythmia with regular intake above ~100 mg glycyrrhizin/day (about 50 g black licorice candy) - FDA has warned adults over 40
Dangerous with diuretics, digoxin (hypokalaemia), corticosteroids, antihypertensives
Avoid in heart failure, kidney disease, hypertension
Pregnancy: heavy use linked to preterm birth and later cognitive effects - avoid
Inhibits CYP3A4 (glabridin) in vitro
herbs.element_or_dosha: TCM (gan cao): sweet, neutral; harmonizes all herbs in a formula, tonifies Spleen qi, moistens Lung. Ayurveda (yashtimadhu): madhura rasa, sheeta virya; pacifies Vata and Pitta.
herbs.folk_correspondence: Mercury (Culpeper, 'Liquorice... under the dominion of Mercury')

herbs.name: Astragalus (Huang Qi)
uses: adjunct in chemotherapy and kidney disease (TCM practice)
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Cycloastragenol is reported to activate telomerase in cell studies (the basis of anti-ageing marketing - unproven in humans); polysaccharides stimulate macrophage and T-cell cytokine release.
herbs.evidence_note: NCCIH rates human evidence as insufficient; many positive trials are small, Chinese-language, and of low methodological quality.
herbs.dose: 9-30 g dried root per day decocted (TCM standard range), or 500 mg-1 g extract 2-3 times daily.
warnings: Immunosuppressants (ciclosporin, tacrolimus) and autoimmune disease: theoretical opposition
May interact with lithium (diuretic effect may raise levels)
Some Astragalus species (locoweeds, not A. membranaceus) are toxic - buy correct species
Insufficient pregnancy data
herbs.element_or_dosha: TCM: sweet, slightly warm; tonifies Spleen and Lung qi, raises yang, consolidates wei qi (exterior).

herbs.name: Ginkgo
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Ginkgolide B antagonises platelet-activating factor (PAF) receptors; ginkgo induces CYP2C19 (lowers omeprazole levels) and has variable CYP3A4 effects.
herbs.evidence_note: Cochrane found no convincing evidence that ginkgo works for dementia or cognitive impairment, and the large GEM trial found no prevention of dementia; modest evidence for claudication walking distance.
herbs.dose: 120-240 mg/day standardized leaf extract (EGb 761: 24% flavone glycosides, 6% terpene lactones) in 2-3 divided doses.
warnings: Bleeding: case reports of intracranial haemorrhage; caution with warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel, NSAIDs; stop 36 h-2 weeks before surgery
Seeds (raw or many roasted) contain ginkgotoxin (4'-O-methylpyridoxine), an anti-vitamin B6 that causes seizures
Seizure threshold: caution with epilepsy
Lowers omeprazole and possibly efavirenz levels (CYP2C19/3A4)
Raw leaf/tea contains allergenic ginkgolic acids
herbs.element_or_dosha: TCM (bai guo = seed; yin xing ye = leaf): seed sweet, bitter, astringent, neutral, slightly toxic; stabilises Lung qi and stops wheezing.

herbs.name: Black Seed (Habbatus Sauda)
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Thymoquinone inhibits 5-LOX and COX (leukotriene and prostaglandin reduction) and NF-kB, and inhibits CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 in vitro and in animal models.
herbs.evidence_note: A 2022 systematic review of 17 clinical studies found consistent modest HbA1c and glucose reductions, and smaller trials show lipid and BP effects; most trials are small, short and use uncharacterised products. Seeds were found in Tutankhamun's tomb, and a hadith calls it 'a cure for every disease except death'.
herbs.dose: Ground seed 1-3 g/day (diabetes trials often 2 g/day), or seed oil 1-3 mL (about 1 tsp) daily, for 8-12 weeks.
warnings: May lower blood sugar and blood pressure - additive with diabetes and BP drugs
Antiplatelet effect - caution with anticoagulants
Topical oil: allergic contact dermatitis reported
Pregnancy: high doses inhibit uterine contraction in animal studies - avoid medicinal doses
Case reports of acute kidney injury at high doses; CYP2C9/3A4 inhibition (e.g. with warfarin, cyclosporine)
herbs.element_or_dosha: Unani (shuneez/kalonji): hot and dry in third degree. Ayurveda (krishna jiraka/upakunchika): katu and tikta rasa, ushna virya; pacifies Kapha and Vata.

herbs.name: Sage (with note on Rosemary)
herbs.latin: Salvia officinalis (rosemary: Salvia rosmarinus, syn. Rosmarinus officinalis)
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Sage inhibits acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase (the basis of the cholinergic memory trials); thujone is a GABA-A antagonist, which is why concentrated oils are convulsant; carnosic acid in both sage and rosemary is a potent lipid antioxidant (Nrf2 activator).
herbs.evidence_note: Small RCTs show sage improves menopausal hot flushes and short-term memory in healthy and mild-Alzheimer's subjects, and EMA accepts traditional use for sweating and throat inflammation; rosemary's cognitive claims rest on very small studies.
herbs.dose: Gargle: 2-3 g dried leaf in 150 mL water, several times daily. Hot flushes/sweating: 1-2 g leaf as tea up to 3 times daily or 300 mg extract daily. Limit to 2 weeks for internal use (EMA) because of thujone. Rosemary tea: 4-6 g leaf/day (EMA).
warnings: Sage essential oil / concentrated extracts can cause seizures (thujone) - never ingest the oil; avoid in epilepsy
Pregnancy and breast-feeding: avoid medicinal doses (thujone; sage dries milk)
May lower blood sugar; anticholinergic/cholinergic drug interactions possible
Rosemary: large amounts may be uterotonic in pregnancy; oil is convulsant in excess
herbs.element_or_dosha: Unani (sage, salbia): hot and dry.
herbs.folk_correspondence: Sage: Jupiter (Culpeper, 'Jupiter claims this... good for the liver, and to breed blood'); Rosemary: Sun, in Aries (Culpeper, 'The Sun claims privilege in it, and it is under the celestial Ram')

herbs.name: Fenugreek
herbs.enzyme_mechanism: Galactomannan fibre slows carbohydrate absorption and 4-hydroxyisoleucine stimulates glucose-dependent insulin secretion; extracts inhibit intestinal alpha-amylase and alpha-glucosidase.
herbs.evidence_note: Meta-analyses show modest fasting glucose and HbA1c reductions; evidence for increasing breast milk is weak and inconsistent. EMA accepts traditional use for appetite loss and topically for minor inflammation.
herbs.dose: Diabetes trials: 5-25 g seed powder daily with meals (often 10 g soaked seed), or 1 g hydroalcoholic extract daily. EMA appetite: 1-6 g seed per day. Topical poultice: 50 g powdered seed in 250 mL water.
warnings: Hypoglycaemia with insulin and diabetes drugs - monitor glucose
May enhance warfarin effect (case reports)
Pregnancy: uterine stimulant - avoid medicinal doses
Peanut/chickpea (legume) cross-allergy
Maple-syrup odour of sweat and urine (can mimic maple-syrup urine disease in newborns of nursing mothers)
Fibre can reduce absorption of oral drugs - separate by 2 h
herbs.element_or_dosha: Ayurveda (methi): katu and tikta rasa, ushna virya; pacifies Vata and Kapha, can raise Pitta. Unani (hulba): hot and dry in second degree. TCM (hu lu ba): bitter, warm; warms kidney yang.
herbs.folk_correspondence: No Culpeper entry of its own (used as an ingredient in his poultices); modern lists assign Mercury

gems.name: Amethyst
gems.mineral: Quartz, SiO2 (trigonal tectosilicate); purple colour from Fe3+ colour centres activated by natural irradiation; Mohs 7.
gems.traditional_correspondences: Greek amethystos = 'not intoxicated' - worn or used as a drinking vessel against drunkenness; associated with Bacchus/Dionysus myth (Renaissance retelling); modern New-Age: crown chakra, Jupiter/Neptune, Pisces and Aquarius; February birthstone; bishops' rings in Christian tradition.
gems.history: Amethyst was carved into beads and amulets in Predynastic and Middle Kingdom Egypt (mined at Wadi el-Hudi) and was among the 'cardinal gems' ranked with diamond and ruby until large Brazilian deposits made it common in the 19th century.
gems.evidence: tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
gems.safety: Chemically inert and insoluble; safe to handle and in water. Colour fades with prolonged sunlight or heat.

gems.name: Rose Quartz
gems.mineral: Quartz, SiO2; pink colour mostly from microscopic fibrous inclusions of a dumortierite-related borosilicate; usually massive, cloudy; Mohs 7.
gems.traditional_correspondences: Modern New-Age: heart chakra, Venus, Taurus and Libra, 'stone of love'; ancient-use claims (Egyptian face masks, Eros myth) circulate online but are not well documented.
gems.history: Rose quartz was carved into snuff bottles, vessels and figures in Qing-dynasty China and became a popular bead and cabochon material worldwide from the 19th-20th centuries.
gems.evidence: tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
gems.safety: Inert and insoluble; safe in water. Pink colour can fade in strong sunlight. Facial rollers are fine if cleaned; many cheap 'rose quartz' items are dyed glass.

gems.name: Clear Quartz (Rock Crystal)
gems.mineral: Quartz, SiO2 (trigonal); colourless; piezoelectric - used as oscillators in watches and radios; Mohs 7.
gems.traditional_correspondences: Greek krystallos ('ice') - Pliny believed it was permanently frozen ice; scrying spheres; modern New-Age: crown chakra, 'master healer', Sun/Moon; used as a sacred stone by many Indigenous Australian and American cultures.
gems.history: Rock crystal was carved into Fatimid Egyptian ewers (10th-11th c.) and medieval reliquaries, and its piezoelectric property (discovered by the Curies in 1880) makes it the real 'crystal technology' in every quartz clock.
gems.evidence: tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims); its piezoelectricity is real physics but does not translate to body healing
gems.safety: Inert and safe in water. Clear spheres can focus sunlight and start fires - keep out of windowsills. Cutting/grinding produces respirable crystalline silica dust (silicosis risk) - wet-cut with a respirator.

gems.name: Citrine
gems.mineral: Quartz, SiO2; yellow to orange from trace iron; natural citrine is rare - most commercial 'citrine' is heat-treated amethyst or smoky quartz; Mohs 7.
gems.traditional_correspondences: Modern New-Age: solar plexus chakra, Sun, Gemini/Leo, 'merchant's stone' for prosperity; November birthstone (with topaz).
gems.history: Citrine was long confused with topaz in trade, and Art Deco jewellers of the 1920s-30s popularised large heat-treated Brazilian citrines.
gems.evidence: tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
gems.safety: Inert; safe in water. Heat-treated material can fade in prolonged sun.

gems.name: Lapis Lazuli
gems.mineral: A rock, not a single mineral: mainly lazurite (Na,Ca)8(AlSiO4)6(S,SO4,Cl)2 (feldspathoid, sodalite group) with white calcite, pyrite flecks, diopside and sodalite; Mohs 5-5.5.
gems.traditional_correspondences: Sumerian: in 'Inanna's Descent' the goddess carries a lapis-lazuli measuring rod and line and wears lapis beads, stripped from her at the underworld gates; Egyptian: the gods' hair was said to be of lapis (Ra's in the Book of the Heavenly Cow), used in Tutankhamun's funerary mask and scarabs; Abrahamic: the sapphire (sappir) of the Bible is often identified with lapis; modern: throat and third-eye chakras, Jupiter/Venus.
gems.history: Nearly all ancient lapis came from the Sar-i Sang mines in Badakhshan, Afghanistan, traded 2,500+ km to the Royal Tombs of Ur (c. 2600 BCE) and to Egypt; ground and purified, it became ultramarine, the most expensive pigment of Renaissance painting.
gems.evidence: tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
gems.safety: Not for gem waters or elixirs: calcite dissolves in acidic water, pyrite oxidises, and lazurite releases hydrogen sulfide in acid. Often dyed or reconstituted - colour can rub off. Avoid acids and ultrasonic cleaners.

gems.name: Carnelian
gems.mineral: Chalcedony (microcrystalline quartz), SiO2, coloured orange-red by iron oxides (hematite/goethite); often heat-enhanced; Mohs 6.5-7.
gems.traditional_correspondences: Egyptian: red stones like carnelian were linked with the blood of Isis (tyet amulet) and with life/vitality; heart amulets and inlay in Tutankhamun's jewellery; Islamic: Prophet's signet ring tradition (aqiq); modern: sacral chakra, Mars/Sun, Leo/Virgo.
gems.history: Carnelian was the most common gemstone of ancient Egypt, and the Harappan (Indus Valley) civilisation exported distinctive etched carnelian beads to Mesopotamia by about 2500 BCE.
gems.evidence: tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
gems.safety: Inert; safe in water. Much modern 'carnelian' is dyed agate.

gems.name: Turquoise
gems.mineral: Hydrated copper aluminium phosphate, CuAl6(PO4)4(OH)8·4H2O (triclinic); porous; Mohs 5-6.
gems.traditional_correspondences: Egyptian: Hathor was 'Lady of Turquoise' (nebet mefkat), worshipped at the turquoise mines of Serabit el-Khadim in Sinai; Persian: Nishapur turquoise as a protective stone; Aztec: xihuitl, sacred to the fire god Xiuhtecuhtli, used in mosaic masks; Diné (Navajo) and Puebloan sacred stone of sky and water; modern: throat chakra, Jupiter/Venus, Sagittarius; December birthstone.
gems.history: Egyptians mined Sinai turquoise from the First Dynasty onward, and the Hathor temple at Serabit el-Khadim holds the Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions, among the earliest alphabetic writing.
gems.evidence: tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
gems.safety: Contains copper - do not make gem waters or elixirs. Porous: absorbs oils, perfume and skin acids and changes colour; most market turquoise is stabilised with resin, dyed, or is dyed howlite/magnesite.

gems.name: Obsidian
gems.mineral: Natural volcanic glass, amorphous (not a mineral), roughly 70-75% SiO2 rhyolitic composition; conchoidal fracture; Mohs 5-5.5.
gems.traditional_correspondences: Aztec: Tezcatlipoca ('Smoking Mirror') and obsidian scrying mirrors; Elizabethan magus John Dee's 'magic mirror' (now in the British Museum) is Aztec obsidian from Pachuca, Mexico; modern: root chakra, Saturn/Pluto, Scorpio, 'protection' stone.
gems.history: Obsidian was the premier blade material of the Stone Age, traded across the Neolithic Near East from Anatolian sources, and Mesoamerican macuahuitl swords were edged with it; a 2021 study confirmed John Dee's mirror is Mexican obsidian.
gems.evidence: tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims); obsidian blade edges are genuinely sharper than steel scalpels and have been trialled in surgery
gems.safety: Fractured edges are razor-sharp; knapping throws glass shards - eye protection and gloves; glass dust is irritating. Inert in water.

gems.name: Moonstone
gems.mineral: Feldspar - microscopic intergrowth of orthoclase (KAlSi3O8) and albite (NaAlSi3O8) layers that scatter light (adularescence); Mohs 6-6.5, perfect cleavage.
gems.traditional_correspondences: Moon; Roman belief (Pliny) that it formed from solidified moonlight and changed with lunar phases; in India regarded as sacred and auspicious; modern: crown/sacral chakra, Cancer; June birthstone (with pearl and alexandrite).
gems.history: Romans used moonstone in jewellery believing it was moonlight made solid, and Art Nouveau jewellers such as Rene Lalique made it fashionable around 1900; Sri Lanka has been the classic source.
gems.evidence: tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
gems.safety: Inert and safe in water, but cleaves easily - avoid knocks, heat and ultrasonic cleaners.

gems.name: Malachite
gems.mineral: Copper carbonate hydroxide, Cu2CO3(OH)2 (monoclinic carbonate); banded green; Mohs 3.5-4; soluble in acids.
gems.traditional_correspondences: Egyptian: ground malachite was green eye paint (wadj) with protective meaning, and Hathor was also called 'Lady of Malachite' at Sinai; Venus/copper association in alchemy; modern: heart chakra, Scorpio/Capricorn, 'protection' stone.
gems.history: Malachite was among the first copper ores smelted (Sinai, Timna, 4th millennium BCE), and Russian Ural malachite veneered the Malachite Room of the Winter Palace, St Petersburg.
gems.evidence: tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
gems.safety: TOXIC: never make malachite gem waters or elixirs, and never ingest - it releases soluble copper in acidic liquids (vomiting, liver/kidney damage). Cutting or polishing dust is a copper inhalation hazard - wet-work and respirator. Finished, sealed jewellery is fine to wear; keep away from water, acids and perfume.

gems.name: Garnet
gems.mineral: Group of nesosilicates X3Y2(SiO4)3 - e.g. pyrope Mg3Al2(SiO4)3, almandine Fe3Al2(SiO4)3, spessartine, grossular, andradite (demantoid), uvarovite; cubic; Mohs 6.5-7.5.
gems.traditional_correspondences: Name from Latin granatum (pomegranate seed); legend that Noah lit the Ark with a garnet; carbuncle of the Bible; modern: root chakra, Mars, Capricorn/Aquarius; January birthstone.
gems.history: Garnet cloisonne set in gold is the signature of Anglo-Saxon royal treasure at Sutton Hoo and in the Staffordshire Hoard, much of it from garnets traded from India and Sri Lanka.
gems.evidence: tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
gems.safety: Insoluble and inert; safe in water. Industrial garnet abrasive dust should not be inhaled.

gems.name: Jade (Nephrite and Jadeite)
gems.mineral: Two different minerals: nephrite, an amphibole (tremolite-actinolite, Ca2(Mg,Fe)5Si8O22(OH)2), Mohs 6-6.5, extremely tough; and jadeite, a pyroxene (NaAlSi2O6), Mohs 6.5-7.
gems.traditional_correspondences: Chinese yu: the 'stone of heaven', embodying Confucian virtues (benevolence, integrity, wisdom), bi discs (heaven) and cong tubes (earth) in Neolithic burials, Han jade burial suits; Maori pounamu (nephrite) taonga; Olmec and Maya jadeite as breath/soul; modern: heart chakra, Venus, Taurus/Libra.
gems.history: Liangzhu culture carved nephrite cong and bi around 3300-2300 BCE without metal tools, and the British Museum holds a cong of c. 2500 BCE; jadeite from Burma only reached China in the 18th century.
gems.evidence: tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
gems.safety: Inert and safe in water. Many 'jade' pieces are dyed or polymer-impregnated (B/C-grade) or are serpentine, aventurine or glass. Cutting raw nephrite/tremolite: wet-cut, as fibrous amphibole dust is a lung hazard.

gems.name: Emerald
gems.mineral: Beryl, Be3Al2Si6O18 (hexagonal cyclosilicate) coloured green by chromium and/or vanadium; Mohs 7.5-8 but brittle with inclusions ('jardin').
gems.traditional_correspondences: Venus; Egyptian 'Cleopatra's mines' (Mons Smaragdus, Wadi Sikait) in the Eastern Desert; Inca and Muisca sacred stone (Colombian Muzo/Chivor); Islamic Mughal carved emeralds with Quranic verses; the 'Emerald Tablet' of Hermes Trismegistus; modern: heart chakra, Taurus/Cancer; May birthstone.
gems.history: Emeralds were mined in Egypt's Eastern Desert from the Ptolemaic and Roman period, but after the Spanish conquest Colombian emeralds flooded Mughal India and Ottoman Turkey.
gems.evidence: tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
gems.safety: Most emeralds are oiled or resin-filled - avoid hot water, solvents, ultrasonic and steam cleaning. Beryl contains beryllium: cutting dust is hazardous (berylliosis) - lapidary only with wet methods and extraction; handling finished stones is safe.

gems.name: Bloodstone (Heliotrope)
gems.mineral: Dark-green chalcedony or jasper (cryptocrystalline SiO2) coloured by chlorite/hornblende inclusions, with red spots of iron oxide (hematite); Mohs 6.5-7.
gems.traditional_correspondences: Greek heliotropion ('sun-turner'): Pliny wrote that in water it turns sunlight blood-red; Christian legend that the red spots are drops of Christ's blood at the Crucifixion (carved into martyr cameos); Babylonian seals; modern: root/heart chakra, Mars, Aries/Pisces; March birthstone (with aquamarine).
gems.history: Bloodstone, chiefly from the Deccan Traps of India, was carved as seals and signet rings from antiquity and as devotional cameos of the Passion in medieval and Renaissance Europe.
gems.evidence: tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims); its old use to 'stop bleeding' has no basis

diagrams.title: The Seven Planets: metals, gems and herbs
diagrams.teaches: How the classical correspondence system links each planet to a metal, a Navaratna gem, a weekday, a god in four cultures and Culpeper's herbs.
diagrams.evidence: tradition (correspondence system; not a medical claim)

diagrams.title: The liver's enzyme crossroads (CYP450)
diagrams.teaches: Why herbs interact with drugs: inducers (St John's wort -> CYP3A4/P-gp up, drugs fail) vs inhibitors (grapefruit, goldenseal, piperine, high-dose curcumin -> drug levels rise).

diagrams.title: TCM Five Phases (Wu Xing)
diagrams.teaches: Wood-Liver, Fire-Heart, Earth-Spleen, Metal-Lung, Water-Kidney; herbs are classed by nature (cold-hot) and five flavours.

diagrams.title: Ayurveda: the three doshas
diagrams.teaches: Vata, Pitta, Kapha and the six tastes (rasa); how warming herbs (ginger) and cooling herbs (amla, coriander) are chosen.

diagrams.title: Unani / Galenic four humours
diagrams.teaches: Unani Tibb (Ibn Sina's Canon) classes herbs as hot/cold and dry/moist by degree; black seed, rose, fennel, senna.

diagrams.title: Enzymes in the kitchen
diagrams.teaches: Proteolytic food enzymes: bromelain (pineapple), papain (papaya), actinidin (kiwi), zingibain (ginger); honey's glucose oxidase makes hydrogen peroxide (why honey dressings work).

diagrams.title: The old wives' medicine cabinet
diagrams.teaches: Folk remedies with real support: honey for cough (not under 1 year), ginger for nausea, peppermint oil for IBS, clove (eugenol) for toothache, salt-water gargle, aloe for minor burns.
diagrams.evidence: mixed: several established, see each herb card

diagrams.title: How it all goes together
diagrams.teaches: Plants = chemistry you can test; gems and planets = the symbolic grammar old healers used to remember it; gods = the stories that carried the knowledge.
diagrams.evidence: framework; chemistry claims are on the herb cards

diagrams.title: A sleep tea, taken apart
diagrams.teaches: Chamomile (apigenin, GABA-A), lemon balm (rosmarinic acid, GABA-transaminase inhibition), valerian (valerenic acid); additive with sedatives and alcohol.

diagrams.title: The doctrine of signatures (and why it misleads)
diagrams.teaches: Paracelsus/Boehme: a plant's shape shows its use. Historically important, medically unreliable; a teaching card on testing claims.

diagrams.title: Hathor's herb index
diagrams.teaches: Ask Hathor: every card links to the wiki article with doses, sources and interaction warnings.
